lead: Hamming codes add a few extra bits to a data word so that a single‑bit error can be detected and corrected without retransmission. This capability is useful on noisy links such as wireless or power‑line channels, where a corrupted frame must be fixed quickly. The (7,4) Hamming code is the smallest practical example and forms the basis for many error‑correction schemes used in storage devices and satellite links.
prereq: You need: error detection basics from Error detection.

blocks.text: A (7,4) Hamming code maps 4 data bits to a 7‑bit code word. The positions that are powers of two (1, 2, 4) hold parity bits p1, p2, p3. The remaining positions (3, 5, 6, 7) hold the data bits d1‑d4. Each parity bit checks a subset of the code word; the subsets are chosen so that the binary representation of the checked positions contains a 1 in the bit corresponding to that parity.

items: Write the 4 data bits in positions 3,5,6,7.
Compute p1 as XOR of bits whose index has LSB = 1 (positions 1,3,5,7).
Compute p2 as XOR of bits whose index has second LSB = 1 (positions 2,3,6,7).
Compute p3 as XOR of bits whose index has third LSB = 1 (positions 4,5,6,7).

blocks.where: ⊕ is XOR; d1 is bit 3, d2 is bit 5, d4 is bit 7.
p3 = d2 ⊕ d3 ⊕ d4 where: d2 is bit 5, d3 is bit 6, d4 is bit 7.

blocks.text: When a code word arrives, the receiver recomputes the three parity checks using the received bits. The three results form the syndrome S = (s3 s2 s1) where s1 is the result of the p1 check, s2 of p2, and s3 of p3. If S = 000 the word is error‑free. Any non‑zero syndrome gives the binary index of the erroneous bit, which can then be flipped to recover the original data.

items: Re‑compute the three parity checks on the received 7 bits.
Form the syndrome S = s3s2s1 (most significant bit from p3).
Otherwise, interpret S as a binary index (1‑7) and invert that bit.
The syndrome works because each parity equation isolates a unique set of positions.
Only a single‑bit error can be corrected; two‑bit errors may produce a valid but wrong syndrome.

blocks.text: Some curricula add an overall parity bit to the (7,4) code, creating an (8,4) code that can correct a single‑bit error and also detect any double‑bit error. The extra parity bit checks all seven bits. If the syndrome is non‑zero but the overall parity is satisfied, the error is a double‑bit error and the receiver must request retransmission.

items: Used in memory modules (ECC RAM) and some storage devices.

examples.question: A sender wants to transmit the 4‑bit data word 1011 using a (7,4) Hamming code. (a) Compute the three parity bits and write the 7‑bit code word. (b) During transmission bit 3 flips. The receiver obtains 0100011. Perform syndrome decoding and state the corrected data bits.
steps: Place data bits: d1=1 (pos3), d2=0 (pos5), d3=1 (pos6), d4=1 (pos7).
Encoded word = p1 p2 d1 p3 d2 d3 d4 = 0 1 1 0 0 1 1 → 0110011.
Syndrome = s3s2s1 = 0 1 1 = binary 3 → error at position 3.
examples.check:
bits = [0,1,0,0,0,1,1]
# recompute syndrome
p1_check = bits[0] ^ bits[2] ^ bits[4] ^ bits[6]
p2_check = bits[1] ^ bits[2] ^ bits[5] ^ bits[6]
p3_check = bits[3] ^ bits[4] ^ bits[5] ^ bits[6]
syndrome = (p3_check<<2) | (p2_check<<1) | p1_check
print(syndrome)
# flip if needed
if syndrome != 0:
    bits[syndrome-1] ^= 1
print(bits[2], bits[4], bits[5], bits[6])

traps: Writing the parity bits in the wrong order (p1, p2, p3) gives an incorrect syndrome.
Treating the syndrome bits as (s1s2s3) instead of (s3s2s1) reverses the binary index.
Assuming the code can correct two‑bit errors; it can only detect them in the extended (8,4) version.
Forgetting that positions are 1‑based when locating the error from the syndrome.

quiz.q: How many parity bits does a (7,4) Hamming code use?
Why are the parity‑bit positions chosen as powers of two?
quiz.a: Because each power‑of‑two position has a unique binary representation, allowing each parity check to correspond to one bit of the syndrome.

quiz.q: Encode the data word 1100 using the (7,4) Hamming code.
A received word is 1011010. Perform syndrome decoding and give the corrected data bits.
quiz.a: Compute s1=1⊕1⊕0⊕0=0, s2=0⊕1⊕1⊕0=0, s3=1⊕0⊕1⊕0=0 → syndrome 000, no error. Data bits = positions 3,5,6,7 = 1 0 1 0.

quiz.q: Explain how the (8,4) SEC‑DED code can detect but not correct a double‑bit error.
quiz.a: If a double‑bit error occurs, the three‑bit syndrome will be non‑zero, but the overall parity check will be satisfied (even). This indicates a double‑bit error, which can be detected but not corrected, so the receiver must request retransmission.

beyond: Not for the exam. In modern data centers, Hamming‑type codes are embedded in ECC memory modules to protect against soft errors caused by cosmic rays. Research extends the idea to low‑density parity‑check (LDPC) codes used in 5G and Wi‑Fi 6 for higher throughput. Look for publications on polar codes and fountain codes as the next step after linear block codes.
